\title{No Peeking: A Self-Refreshing Benchmark for Look-Ahead Bias in LLM Forecasts of Market Reactions to Corporate Filings}

\author{K\'evin Feltrin\\
  ESIEE Paris, Universit\'e Gustave Eiffel\\
  \url{https://github.com/KvnFltr/no-peeking}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to read corporate disclosures and forecast how markets will
react, but their apparent skill is hard to trust: their pre-training corpora contain the very outcomes they are
asked to predict. We introduce \dataset{}, a benchmark of SEC Form 8-K filings paired with the market-adjusted
stock reaction that followed, built entirely from public data by an open pipeline that appends new filings every
month. Its headline test split only contains filings published after the release of every model we evaluate, so it
cannot have been memorized. We use it for two studies. First, a \emph{look-ahead probe} that crosses the period
(before vs.\ after the training cutoff) with the text (original vs.\ anonymized) and estimates memorization as a
difference-in-differences, with a non-memorizing text classifier as a control. Second, a controlled study of
post-training small models (0.5B--1.5B parameters, trainable on free GPUs) to reason about filings:
\emph{hindsight distillation}, in which a teacher sees the realized outcome and writes the reasoning an analyst
could have written beforehand, compared with outcome-blind rationales, preference optimization, and GRPO with a
proper-scoring (Brier) reward and a grounding reward that checks cited facts against the filing. We evaluate
discrimination, calibration, faithfulness and a cost-aware long-short portfolio, with bootstrap confidence intervals
and comparisons pre-registered before any model was scored on the test set. Code, data-building scripts, derived
labels and a leaderboard are released.
% The final abstract adds the three headline numbers through macros once the main runs are complete.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A growing literature asks whether LLMs can forecast asset prices from text \citep{lopezlira2023chatgpt,
kim2024financial}. The answer is clouded by \emph{look-ahead bias}: a model pre-trained on news written after the
events in a backtest may ``predict'' outcomes it has read about
\citep{glasserman2023lookahead,sarkar2025lookahead}. \citet{lopezlira2025memorization} show that LLMs reproduce exact
pre-cutoff economic and financial values, that instructions to respect a cutoff do not prevent recall, and that
masking names and dates fails because models reconstruct entities from little context. Proposed remedies include
point-in-time models trained on time-sliced corpora \citep{he2025chronologically}, statistical tests that exploit
unpredictable events \citep{sarkar2025lookahead,gao2025detecting}, and agentic trading benchmarks that measure alpha
decay \citep{benhenda2026lookahead}.

Two gaps remain. (i) There is no public, regularly refreshed benchmark of \emph{text-to-market-reaction} pairs whose
test set is, by construction, posterior to the models being evaluated, together with a simple probe that anyone can
run on any open model. (ii) Work that post-trains LLMs for financial reasoning with reinforcement learning
\citep{liu2025finr1,xiao2025tradingr1} uses 7B+ models and large clusters, and rarely asks the question that matters
for hindsight-based supervision: when a teacher writes rationales \emph{knowing} the outcome, as in STaR's
rationalization step \citep{zelikman2022star}, does the student learn transferable reasoning, or confident stories
that do not survive out of sample?

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{\dataset{}}, a benchmark of 8-K filings (with their Exhibit 99.1 press releases) from S\&P 500 and
  S\&P 400 firms since 2018, labelled with 1- and 3-day returns in excess of SPY, with time-based splits, an embargo
  and a post-cutoff test split that grows monthly. Every filter is logged with counts; raw prices are never
  redistributed (\S\ref{sec:data}).
  \item \textbf{A look-ahead probe} (\texttt{nopeeking probe <model>}) that estimates memorization as a
  difference-in-differences over period $\times$ anonymization, with bootstrap intervals and a text-classifier
  control that cannot remember the test period (\S\ref{sec:probe}).
  \item \textbf{A controlled post-training study} on 0.5B--1.5B students: hindsight vs.\ outcome-blind rationale
  distillation, DPO on correct-vs-wrong rationales, and GRPO with Brier, grounding and format rewards, all under the
  same budget and evaluated for calibration and faithfulness, not only accuracy (\S\ref{sec:posttrain}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Look-ahead bias and memorization.}
\citet{glasserman2023lookahead} compare GPT-3.5 sentiment strategies on original and anonymized headlines and find a
``distraction'' effect alongside look-ahead bias. \citet{sarkar2025lookahead} test for leakage with events that
should be unpredictable from a given information set; \citet{gao2025detecting} propose a further statistical test for
LLM forecasts; \citet{lopezlira2025memorization} document verbatim recall of pre-cutoff macroeconomic and market
values; \citet{he2025chronologically} train chronologically consistent models; and Look-Ahead-Bench
\citep{benhenda2026lookahead} measures alpha decay of LLM trading agents on a handful of large stocks. We complement
these with a filing-level, multi-thousand-firm benchmark whose test split is posterior to model release, and with an
anonymization difference-in-differences that separates recall from the information removed by masking.

\paragraph{Text and stock returns.}
Media tone predicts returns \citep{tetlock2007giving}; finance-specific dictionaries \citep{loughran2011liability} and
models such as FinBERT \citep{araci2019finbert} improved text measures; \citet{lee2014importance} predicted the
reaction to 8-K events from their text. Event-study conventions follow \citet{mackinlay1997event}.

\paragraph{Contamination-free evaluation.}
Dynamic benchmarks avoid contamination by asking about information that did not exist at training time
\citep{white2024livebench,karger2025forecastbench}; \citet{golchin2024time} trace contamination of static test sets.
\dataset{} applies the same principle to financial disclosures, with a monthly refresh.

\paragraph{Post-training for reasoning.}
STaR \citep{zelikman2022star} generates rationales conditioned on the answer (``rationalization''); DPO
\citep{rafailov2023dpo} and GRPO \citep{shao2024deepseekmath} are the standard preference and RL objectives, used for
financial reasoning by Fin-R1 \citep{liu2025finr1} and for trading by Trading-R1 \citep{xiao2025tradingr1}.
Binary outcome rewards degrade calibration, which Brier-score rewards repair \citep{damani2026beyond}; with noisy or
weakly informative rewards, RL gains can be spurious \citep{shao2026spurious}, a central risk for market labels.

\section{\dataset{}}
\label{sec:data}

\paragraph{Sources and universe.}
We take the current constituents of the S\&P 500 and S\&P 400, map them to SEC central index keys, and list every Form
8-K (amendments excluded) since 1 January 2018 from the EDGAR submissions API, which records the exact acceptance
timestamp of each filing. Requests declare a contact and stay below the SEC fair-access limit.
For each filing we extract the text of the 8-K items and of Exhibit 99.1 (usually the press release), remove inline
XBRL headers, hidden content and the legal boilerplate common to every filing (furnished-not-filed notices,
forward-looking-statement disclaimers), and keep the first 20{,}000 characters.

\paragraph{Events.}
The event type follows the 8-K items, by priority: results of operations (item 2.02), material agreements and
acquisitions or dispositions (1.01, 2.01), executive and director changes (5.02), and other events (8.01). Filings
without any of these items are excluded. One filing is kept per firm and event day.

\paragraph{Timing and labels.}
The event day $t$ is the first trading session whose 16:00 ET close is strictly after the EDGAR acceptance time, so a
filing accepted at 16:30 is assigned to the next session. With $P$ adjusted closes, the $h$-day market-adjusted return
is
\begin{equation}
  r^{\mathrm{adj}}_{i,h} = \frac{P_{i,t+h-1}}{P_{i,t-1}} - \frac{P_{\mathrm{SPY},t+h-1}}{P_{\mathrm{SPY},t-1}},
  \qquad h\in\{1,3\}.
\end{equation}
The primary target is $y=\mathbf{1}[r^{\mathrm{adj}}_{i,3}>0]$; secondary targets are the 1-day sign and terciles.
Winsorization (1\%/99\%) and tercile cut-offs are estimated on the training split only.

\paragraph{Splits.}
Training: 2018--2022. Pre-cutoff test: 2023, used \emph{only} to measure memorization. Validation: 2024, used for all
tuning. An embargo removes January--June 2025. Post-cutoff test: from 1 July 2025, i.e.\ after the release of every
model studied here; it grows each month as new filings complete their 3-day window.

\paragraph{The released version.}
The frozen snapshot used in this paper (v1) samples filings per split from the 899-firm universe
(Table~\ref{tab:data}); the pipeline also builds the full universe. Table~\ref{tab:filterlog} in the appendix gives
the count after every filter.

\section{The look-ahead probe}
\label{sec:probe}

For a model $M$ we score each test filing with one forward pass: given the filing and the question ``will the stock
outperform the S\&P 500 over the next 3 trading days?'', $\hat p = P_M(\texttt{Yes})/(P_M(\texttt{Yes})+P_M(\texttt{No}))$
at the first answer token. Each filing is scored twice: with the original text and header (company, ticker, date),
and with an anonymized version in which company names, tickers, dates, years, URLs and file names are masked.
Let $A_{p,v}$ be the AUC on period $p\in\{\text{pre},\text{post}\}$ and version $v\in\{\text{orig},\text{anon}\}$.
Masking removes some legitimate information in both periods, but recall can only help on original pre-cutoff
filings, so we estimate memorization by
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{DiD} = (A_{\text{pre},\text{orig}} - A_{\text{pre},\text{anon}}) - (A_{\text{post},\text{orig}} - A_{\text{post},\text{anon}}).
\end{equation}
Confidence intervals come from 2{,}000 bootstrap resamples of filings, paired across versions and independent across
periods. As a control we report the same quantity for a TF-IDF logistic regression trained on 2018--2022, which cannot
remember 2023 outcomes: its DiD measures what masking does to a non-memorizing reader. The probe does not require
access to the training data and runs on any causal LM on the Hugging Face Hub.

\section{Post-training small models}
\label{sec:posttrain}

\paragraph{Answer format.}
Reasoning models answer with \texttt{Reasoning:}, \texttt{Prediction: Up|Down} and
\texttt{Probability of outperforming: p}, which makes predictions parseable and calibration measurable.

\paragraph{Hindsight distillation.}
A teacher (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 4-bit) receives the filing \emph{and} the realized outcome (direction and size of the
market-adjusted move) and is asked to write the reasoning an analyst could have written before knowing it, citing only
facts in the filing. Rationales are kept only if they parse, predict the conditioning direction, contain no outcome
leakage (a pattern list covering post-filing price moves and hindsight phrasing) and reach a fact precision of at
least 0.8, the share of numbers cited in the reasoning that also appear in the filing. A \emph{control} set is written
with the same prompt but no outcome. Students (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B-Instruct) are fine-tuned with LoRA
\citep{hu2022lora} on each set; a direct-label SFT baseline learns the Yes/No answer only.

\paragraph{Preference optimization.}
DPO pairs, for the same filing, the hindsight rationale for the realized outcome (chosen) with one written for the
opposite outcome (rejected), both passing the filters.

\paragraph{GRPO rewards.}
Starting from the hindsight-SFT adapter we run GRPO \citep{shao2024deepseekmath} with (a) an outcome reward
$R_{\mathrm{out}} = 1-2(\hat p-y)^2$, a bounded proper scoring rule \citep{brier1950verification} that rewards
calibrated rather than merely confident answers \citep{damani2026beyond}; (b) $R_{\mathrm{out}}+0.5\,R_{\mathrm{ground}}$,
where $R_{\mathrm{ground}}$ is the fact precision of the reasoning minus one if it leaks the outcome; and (c) an
additional format reward. All methods share the number of optimizer steps and the effective batch size, and run on a
free Kaggle GPU with TRL \citep{vonwerra2020trl}.

\section{Experimental setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
Zero-shot: Qwen2.5 \citep{qwen2025qwen25} 0.5B--7B and other open instruction models released before July 2025, so
that the post-cutoff test is unseen by all of them. Non-LLM baselines: majority class, event-type prior and TF-IDF
with logistic regression (regularization chosen on validation AUC).

\paragraph{Metrics.}
AUC is the primary metric (base rates move across periods); we also report accuracy, balanced accuracy, the Brier
score, expected calibration error \citep{guo2017calibration} and the rank correlation between $\hat p$ and the realized
(winsorized) return. Faithfulness is measured by fact precision and the leak rate of generated reasoning.

\paragraph{Portfolio.}
On the post-cutoff test, each filing with a score in the top (bottom) tercile of validation scores opens a long
(short) position at the first close after the filing, the close of day $t$, and holds it for the two remaining
sessions of the window, hedged with SPY, equally weighted within legs, with 5 bps per side. The day-$t$ reaction is
part of the prediction target but cannot be traded with daily closes; an earlier version of our simulator entered at
the close of $t-1$, before the filing was public, and overstated the Sharpe ratio, a look-ahead error caught before
any language model was evaluated. We report
the annualized Sharpe ratio with a circular block bootstrap interval \citep{politis1992circular}. The portfolio is
reported for every method and never used for selection.

\paragraph{Pre-registration.}
Splits, metrics, primary comparisons and the budget rule were committed to the repository before any model was
scored on a test split; deviations are listed in its changelog.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
The universe is today's index membership, which induces survivorship bias in early years. Anonymization masks names,
tickers and dates but not executives, products or distinctive numbers, so identity can survive masking; the DiD is a
lower bound on recall when masking is incomplete. Daily close-to-close returns include intraday moves before the
filing on day $t$ when a filing is accepted during market hours. Three-day market reactions are noisy, which bounds
achievable accuracy and makes small effects hard to detect; we therefore report intervals rather than point
estimates. We study one market, one horizon family and open models up to 8B parameters.

\section{Broader impact and ethics}
All data are public. Filing texts come from EDGAR, accessed under the SEC fair-access policy with a declared contact;
prices come from a public source and are not redistributed, only derived labels are. The benchmark is meant to make
claims about LLM forecasting more credible; it is not investment advice, and the portfolio results are not a
trading strategy recommendation.

\section*{Reproducibility}
The repository contains the package, configurations, seeds, the pre-registration, a Kaggle notebook that reproduces
the main tables on free GPUs, and the generator of every table, figure and number in this paper.
